findings.F1: The fade shows on the first day only: the short's excess fall over 1 day is +0.89 % (t 2.29, 106 cases, 58 % of them falling), against +0.21 % over 2 days (t 0.31), +0.35 % over 10 days (t 0.23) and +1.26 % over the plan's cut 10-day measure (t 0.97).
findings.F2: After the first day the coin does not keep falling back: from day 1 to day 10 the short's excess is −0.49 % (t −0.33, 106 cases), and over 20 days it is −1.27 % (t −0.63, 102 cases), so the plan's 10-day horizon spreads a one-day move across nine days of noise.
findings.F3: Ordinary falling-month bars fall more than these breaks do. On the 10-day grid of all bars with a negative 30-day return, the short's excess is +1.37 % (t 3.59, 1318 cases), against +0.35 % for the break cases. Over 10 days, a break of a repeatedly-held high in a falling month adds nothing to the month's own continuation, and the market's move drowns it.
findings.F4: On the first day the fall grows with the depth of the 30-day decline. The day-1 excess is +1.17 % for the deepest third (30-day return −10 % to −38 %, t 1.77, 23 cases), +1.15 % for the middle third (t 1.69, 22 cases) and +0.31 % for the shallowest third (−1.5 % to −4.5 %, t 0.39, 23 cases).

ideas.idea: When a coin closes above a price where it turned down several times in the past 90 days while its 30-day return is negative, it tends to fall back over the next day, and the deeper its 30-day decline, the larger that fall.
ideas.consequence: A trader fading a break of a repeatedly-held high in a falling month should take the fade for one day only, larger the deeper the month's decline, and not hold it for a 10-day reversal that does not come.
ideas.name: one-day fade of falling-month breaks
